binders: A graph size n specifying a set of n vertices.
A connection probability p for the Erdos-Renyi model G(n,p).
A random graph G distributed according to G(n,p).
An arbitrary vertex v of G.
hypotheses: For every pair of distinct vertices, the corresponding edge is present with probability p.
The edge choices for distinct vertex pairs are independent.
conclusions: The expected degree of v is (n-1)p.
Because v is arbitrary, every vertex has this same expected degree.
The source introduces d as notation for this common expected degree: d := (n-1)p.
definitions_and_conventions: The degree of a vertex is the number of edges incident to that vertex.
G(n,p) is formed on n vertices by independently connecting each pair of distinct vertices with probability p.
For a fixed vertex, the degree is the sum of the n-1 incident-edge indicators, each distributed as Ber(p).
implicit_context: The construction uses pairs of distinct vertices, so a vertex has exactly n-1 possible incident edges.
As p is called a probability, its intended range is the probability interval, although the displayed expectation sentence does not restate that range.
The claim concerns expectation with respect to the randomness of G sampled from G(n,p).

details: The expectation formula applies to every vertex, not merely to an average over vertices or to a distinguished vertex.
The common value d is determined by n and p rather than independently chosen.
The degree is a random count of incident edges.
For a fixed vertex it has n-1 Bernoulli(p) summands.
Only pairs of distinct vertices are candidates for edges.
All candidate edges have the same inclusion probability p and are mutually independent.
The expected degree is exactly (n-1)p, not an asymptotic estimate or concentration bound.

undebatable_constraints: The graph model must have n vertices and one independent Bernoulli(p) edge choice for each pair of distinct vertices.
Vertex degree must mean the number of incident edges.
The expectation claim must be pointwise for every vertex.
The expected value must equal exactly (n-1)p.
The notation d must denote (n-1)p, the common expected degree.

ambiguities.issue: The displayed sentence does not explicitly state the admissible ranges of n and p.

ambiguities.impact: A formal statement must choose standard domain assumptions, normally a finite n-vertex set and p in the probability interval; edge cases such as an empty vertex set are not discussed by the sentence.

ambiguities.issue: The source uses d both as the name of the common expected degree and later uses d_i for the degree random variable of vertex i.
ambiguities.evidence: PDF page 10; printed page 21 defines (n-1)p =: d, while the first paragraph of the proof of Proposition 2.4.1 denotes the degree of fixed vertex i by d_i.
ambiguities.impact: A formalization should keep the deterministic mean d distinct from the random vertex-degree variable; this is a notation issue, not a mathematical uncertainty in the equality.

contract_plain_english: In an Erdos-Renyi random graph on n vertices, each possible edge between two distinct vertices is included independently with probability p. For any fixed vertex, its degree counts its n-1 possible incident edges, so its expected degree is exactly (n-1)p. This holds for every vertex, and the book calls the common expected degree d.
